java-environment.title: Java Basics & Environment
java-environment.goal: Understand how a Java program runs and print your first message.
java-environment.idea: A Java program is a set of instructions. You write a source file, a compiler checks and translates it into bytecode, and a Java Virtual Machine runs that bytecode.
words: The development kit containing tools such as the Java compiler and launcher.
The virtual machine that executes Java bytecode.
The text you write, normally saved with a .java extension.
focus: Set up a local JDK and editor

concepts.title: Follow source → bytecode → execution
concepts.text: Think of a recipe, its translated instructions, and a cook. Main.java is your recipe; javac produces Main.class; java launches the program on a JVM. The JVM implementation handles differences between operating systems.

concepts.title: Set up a local JDK and editor
concepts.text: For local practice, install a JDK and use an editor such as IntelliJ or VS Code with Java support. Check java -version and javac -version in a new terminal. If the commands are not found, check the JDK installation and PATH. This website’s Playground can run an example without a local setup.

concepts.title: Understand JDK, JRE, and JVM
concepts.text: JRE is the runtime environment concept: the JVM and supporting libraries. The JDK supplies development tools and runtime components. You do not need to hunt for a separate JRE to write programs with a modern JDK.

concepts.title: Read the program frame
concepts.text: In our exercises, save a public class named Main in Main.java. The main method is the entry point used here. Braces group code, a semicolon ends a print statement, and // starts a line comment. Java names are case-sensitive.

example.title: A welcome sign at a college event
example.situation: An event desk wants to print a welcome message followed by the room name.

steps.title: Start at main
steps.text: The JVM starts the entry method. In this example, the first instruction is the welcome print.

steps.title: Print the first line
steps.text: println displays the message and moves to a new line.

steps.title: Print the room
steps.text: The second instruction runs next, in source order.

example.change: Change the room to Room 202. Predict how many output lines there will be before running the program.

check.question: What is the difference between javac Main.java and java Main?
check.answer: javac compiles the source file into bytecode. java launches the compiled Main class on a JVM.

java-environment.remember: Write a small program, run it, read its output, and change one thing at a time.
java-environment.mistake: Use matching capitalization: Main, main, System, and println are different names.
java-environment.ready: You can explain the program frame and print two lines in order.

exception-handling.title: Exception Handling
exception-handling.goal: Understand a failure, catch a specific exception, and choose a useful recovery.
exception-handling.idea: An exception reports that a normal operation could not finish. Handling it means choosing what your program should do after that failure, such as rejecting an invalid number.
words: The block containing an operation that may fail.
The block that handles a matching exception.
throw raises an exception; throws declares that a method may let one reach its caller.

concepts.title: Trace try and catch
concepts.text: If a statement throws an exception, the remaining statements in that try block are skipped. Java looks for a compatible catch. Catch the exception you can handle rather than hiding every failure.

concepts.title: Distinguish checked and unchecked exceptions
concepts.text: Checked exceptions, such as IOException, must be caught or declared with throws. RuntimeException subclasses, such as NumberFormatException, do not have that compiler requirement. A checked exception is still thrown at runtime; it is not a syntax error.

concepts.title: Use finally and automatic closing
concepts.text: finally normally runs when control leaves try/catch, even after an exception or return; it is not guaranteed if the process terminates. For closable resources, prefer try-with-resources so they are closed automatically.

concepts.title: Raise a meaningful error
concepts.text: throw can reject invalid input. A custom exception extends an exception class and should explain the failure. Catch more specific exception types before broader ones.

example.title: Read an age typed at a registration desk
example.situation: The text "twenty" cannot be converted to an integer. Show a helpful message and keep the next instruction reachable.
example.output:
Enter a whole number
Registration is still open

steps.title: Try the conversion
steps.text: parseInt expects numeric text. The word twenty makes it throw NumberFormatException.

steps.title: Handle that failure
steps.text: The matching catch prints the helpful message; the Age line is skipped.

steps.title: Continue afterward
steps.text: The statement after try/catch can still run.

example.change: Change typedAge to "20". Predict which message disappears and which new line appears.

check.question: Does catch run when typedAge is "20"?
check.answer: No. The conversion succeeds, so the try block prints Age: 20. Control then continues after the try/catch.

exception-handling.remember: Handle the failure where you can make a sensible recovery; otherwise let the caller decide.
exception-handling.mistake: Do not use an empty catch block. It makes a failed operation look as if it succeeded.
exception-handling.ready: You can trace both the successful path and the exception path.

collections-framework.title: Collections Framework Overview
collections-framework.goal: Choose a collection from the behavior you need.
collections-framework.idea: Collections are reusable containers. Choose one by asking whether order, duplicates, uniqueness, lookup by key, or the next item to process matters.
words: An ordered sequence that can contain duplicates.
A lookup from each key to its associated value.
focus: Choose List, Set, Map, or Queue
Use a type parameter and wrapper types

concepts.title: Choose List, Set, Map, or Queue
concepts.text: A shopping list needs sequence and duplicates; a visitor register needs unique IDs; a menu needs dish-to-price lookup; a waiting line needs a next item. Map belongs to the framework but does not extend the Collection interface.

concepts.title: Separate interface from implementation
concepts.text: List describes list behavior. ArrayList and LinkedList implement it with different storage and costs. Queue describes processing operations; ArrayDeque gives FIFO behavior when used through Queue, while PriorityQueue chooses by priority.

concepts.title: Use a type parameter and wrapper types
concepts.text: The angle brackets say which element type is allowed. Use Integer instead of int inside a collection type. Generics give compile-time type checks; the dedicated Generics stage explains how to write your own.

concepts.title: Choose ordering and iterate safely
concepts.text: HashMap/HashSet do not promise iteration order. TreeMap/TreeSet keep sorted order; LinkedHashMap/LinkedHashSet preserve insertion order. Use enhanced for to read items and an Iterator when its remove operation is needed.

example.title: Count orders at a tea stall
example.situation: Three orders arrive: Tea, Coffee, Tea. Keep their arrival order, identify unique drinks, and count orders for each drink.

steps.title: Keep the arrivals
steps.text: The list keeps all three orders, including the repeated Tea.

steps.title: Keep distinct drinks
steps.text: The linked set keeps the first occurrence of each drink in arrival order.

steps.title: Count each key
steps.text: The linked map stores one current count per drink. Each new order increases that count.

example.change: Add another Coffee to the order list. Predict the list, set, and map results separately.

check.question: Which collection answers “How many Tea orders?” directly?
check.answer: A Map<String, Integer> holding drink counts. A Set only tells you whether Tea is present.

collections-framework.remember: Choose the container from the question you must answer, then learn its operations.
collections-framework.mistake: Do not assume every collection is sorted or permits duplicates.
collections-framework.ready: You can explain why a list, set, map, and queue solve different jobs.

generics.title: Generics
generics.goal: Use type parameters to make reusable code with checked types.
generics.idea: Generics let a class or method work with a chosen type. A Box<String> promises to hold text, while a Box<Integer> promises to hold integer objects.
words: A placeholder such as T for a type.
The chosen type, such as String.
A restriction on which types a parameter accepts.
focus: Write a class with a type parameter
Use a bound when a capability is required

concepts.title: Write a class with a type parameter
concepts.text: Put <T> after the class name. Use T for fields, parameters, and return values. The same code can then store different types without casting every returned value.

concepts.title: Write a generic method
concepts.text: A method can declare its own type parameter before its return type. Java often infers the type from the call. Generic interfaces use the same idea to describe capabilities for a chosen type.

concepts.title: Use a bound when a capability is required
concepts.text: <T extends Number> permits numeric reference types and lets the method call Number methods. A wildcard ? means an unknown type. ? extends Number is useful for reading numbers; ? super Integer can accept Integer values.

concepts.title: Recognize the limits
concepts.text: Use wrapper types, not primitives: List<Integer>, not List<int>. Avoid raw types such as List without angle brackets. List<Integer> is not a subtype of List<Number>. Java erases most generic type information after compilation.

example.title: Label two storage boxes
example.situation: One box holds a student name and another holds a locker number. The compiler keeps their types separate.

steps.title: Choose each type
steps.text: String replaces T for the name box; Integer replaces it for the locker box.

steps.title: Store the value
steps.text: The constructor accepts a value of the selected type.

steps.title: Retrieve without a cast
steps.text: get returns the selected type. The Integer value is unboxed into int.

example.change: Change the locker box to Box<String> and store "A42". Also change the receiving variable to String.

check.question: Can you construct new Box<String>(42)?
check.answer: No. This box expects a String, so an integer argument produces a compile-time type error.

generics.remember: Generics reuse an implementation while keeping the chosen types consistent.
generics.mistake: Do not remove the type argument just to silence a type error; fix the mismatch.
generics.ready: You can read a generic declaration and create a correctly typed instance.

file-handling.title: File Handling
file-handling.goal: Write and read a text file, then close the resources correctly.
file-handling.idea: File handling moves information between your program and storage. A path identifies a location; readers bring text in and writers send text out.
words: A representation of a file location, not its contents.
Tools for reading and writing characters.
A temporary area that groups I/O work efficiently.
focus: Distinguish a file name from an open file
Read and write text with buffers
Close resources even after a failure

concepts.title: Distinguish a file name from an open file
concepts.text: Creating new File("notes.txt") represents a location; it does not create or read that file by itself. java.nio.file.Path and Files provide modern operations for creating, copying, moving, and deleting files.

concepts.title: Read and write text with buffers
concepts.text: FileReader/FileWriter are character streams. BufferedReader adds operations such as readLine; BufferedWriter supports newLine. For a known text encoding, use an API where you specify it, such as Files.newBufferedReader(path, UTF_8).

concepts.title: Close resources even after a failure
concepts.text: Put readers and writers in try-with-resources. Closing the writer flushes pending data. IOException is checked: catch it meaningfully or declare throws IOException so the caller must handle it.

concepts.title: Treat files and errors carefully
concepts.text: A file can be missing, unreadable, or unwritable. Reading until readLine returns null handles an unknown number of lines. Opening a writer may replace existing contents unless append mode is explicitly selected. Practice with a temporary file you created.

example.title: Save and reload a two-item shopping note
example.situation: Write Tea and Milk to a temporary text file, close it, read both lines, and delete only that temporary file.

steps.title: Create a temporary location
steps.text: createTempFile returns the path of a new temporary file.

steps.title: Write and close
steps.text: The writer stores both items as UTF-8 text and closes before reading starts.

steps.title: Read until the end
steps.text: readLine returns each line without its newline, then null at end-of-file.

steps.title: Clean up the example
steps.text: The final block deletes only the temporary file this program created.

example.change: Add Bread as a third line before the writer closes. The read loop should print all three items.

check.question: Does new File("notes.txt") read the contents of notes.txt?
check.answer: No. It represents a file location. You need a reader or a Files read operation to access the contents.

file-handling.remember: Choose the correct encoding, close what you open, and handle I/O failures.
file-handling.mistake: A remote compiler cannot read a path on your own laptop. Do not put a personal local path in the example.
file-handling.ready: You can explain when a writer closes and why the reader loop stops.
file-handling.runtimeNote: This example creates a temporary file in the compiler environment and deletes it afterward. It does not read your laptop’s files or save a downloadable file. If the compiler restricts file I/O, run this example locally with your JDK.

complexity.title: Time & Space Complexity
complexity.goal: Compare how work and extra memory grow when the input gets larger.
complexity.idea: Complexity describes growth, rather than a stopwatch result. Ask how many operations and how much extra memory a solution needs when the number of inputs doubles.
words: The input size, such as the number of marks.
An asymptotic upper-bound description of growth.
Extra working memory used beyond the input.

concepts.title: Count repeated work
concepts.text: Looking at one fixed array position is O(1). Visiting every element is O(n). Checking every pair is O(n²). Two consecutive full scans are O(n + n), which simplifies to O(n).

concepts.title: Understand halving and sorted input
concepts.text: Binary search discards about half of a sorted search range each step, giving O(log n) search time. Sorting first also has a cost; do not hide that cost when comparing whole solutions.

concepts.title: Count extra memory separately
concepts.text: A loop with only a sum variable uses O(1) auxiliary space. Copying n values uses O(n). A recursive call stack of depth n also uses O(n) space, even without a new array.

concepts.title: Name your assumptions
concepts.text: State whether you mean worst-case, average, or amortized cost. HashMap lookup is expected O(1) with good hash distribution. For a nested loop whose bounds differ, use both sizes, such as O(rows × columns).

example.title: Find the largest daily sale
example.situation: Visit each sale once and keep only the largest seen so far. Count the visits to make the work visible.

steps.title: Remember one candidate
steps.text: Use the first actual value as the initial maximum. This example assumes a nonempty array.

steps.title: Visit each sale
steps.text: The loop makes one pass, updating largest when it finds a bigger value.

steps.title: Compare growth
steps.text: For n sales there are n visits. The counters use constant extra space.

example.change: Add four more sales. Predict the visit count and explain why the algorithm is still O(n).

check.question: Two separate loops each visit n values. Is the total O(n²)?
check.answer: No. They do n + n operations, so the total is O(n). A loop that performs n inner iterations for each of n outer iterations gives O(n²).

complexity.remember: Write time growth and extra-space growth separately, with clear assumptions.
complexity.mistake: Do not label every nested loop O(n²); inspect how many times its bodies actually run.
complexity.ready: You can explain O(1), O(n), O(log n), and O(n²) with a small example.

multithreading.title: Multithreading & Concurrency
multithreading.goal: Understand a thread, wait for its result, and protect shared state.
multithreading.idea: A thread is an independent path of execution. Concurrency lets tasks make progress during the same period; true parallel execution depends on available processors and scheduling.
words: A path of execution inside a process.
A task whose run method has no return value.
Coordination that protects shared state and visibility.
focus: Describe the task and start a thread

concepts.title: Describe the task and start a thread
concepts.text: Implement Runnable for the work. Thread.start schedules a new thread to execute it. Calling run directly is an ordinary method call on the current thread. Extending Thread is another approach, but separating the task from the thread is usually clearer.

concepts.title: Wait using join
concepts.text: join waits for a thread to finish. It can throw InterruptedException. Do not use an arbitrary sleep to assume another thread has finished; scheduling and completion times can change.

concepts.title: Protect a compound update
concepts.text: count++ reads, adds, and writes; it is not one indivisible operation. Two threads can overwrite each other’s updates. A synchronized method uses an object’s monitor so only one thread holds that monitor at a time.

concepts.title: Learn coordination before advanced tools
concepts.text: Shared-state bugs depend on timing. Avoid holding one lock while waiting for work that requires another conflicting lock. Producer/consumer queues, executors, and lock classes are useful next steps. Basic DSA does not require mastery of these tools.

example.title: Two counters record event arrivals
example.situation: Two workers each record 100 arrivals. Both update one synchronized counter. Wait for both workers before printing.

steps.title: Share one counter
steps.text: Both worker tasks refer to the same Counter object.

steps.title: Protect each update
steps.text: synchronized ensures updates on that object cannot overwrite one another.

steps.title: Wait before printing
steps.text: join waits for both sets of 100 updates. Their interleaving can vary, but the final count is 200.

example.change: Change each worker to 150 arrivals. Predict the final count. Keep synchronization and both joins.

check.question: Why is printing immediately after start unreliable?
check.answer: The workers may still be running. join waits for completion so the final result can be read after all updates.

multithreading.remember: Protect shared updates and wait for a result before using it.
multithreading.mistake: Removing synchronized may produce the right answer sometimes; that does not prove the update is safe.
multithreading.ready: You can distinguish start from run and explain why join is needed.
multithreading.runtimeNote: The example uses a short lambda for Runnable; the next stage explains that syntax. Thread scheduling varies, so only the final joined result is displayed.

java8-features.title: Java 8+ Features
java8-features.goal: Read lambdas and a simple stream pipeline without losing the underlying logic.
java8-features.idea: A lambda supplies a small behavior. A stream describes operations over values, such as selecting and transforming them. These features complement the loops and methods you already know.
words: An expression supplying a function-like behavior.
An interface with one abstract method.
A source, intermediate operations, and a terminal operation.
focus: Give an interface a short implementation

concepts.title: Give an interface a short implementation
concepts.text: A lambda matches a functional interface. Predicate<T> tests a value, Function<T,R> transforms it, and Consumer<T> uses it without returning a result. You can first write the equivalent ordinary method to understand the job.

concepts.title: Read filter → map → terminal operation
concepts.text: filter keeps matching values. map transforms each remaining value. Intermediate operations are lazy: a terminal operation such as collect or count triggers processing. A stream is not itself a stored collection.

concepts.title: Recognize method references and collectors
concepts.text: System.out::println passes an existing method as a behavior. Collectors.toList gathers results into a list. Stream operations normally leave the source collection unchanged; avoid shared side effects inside the pipeline.

concepts.title: Use reduce and Optional deliberately
concepts.text: reduce combines values into one result, such as a sum. Some operations return Optional to represent an absent answer. Use an appropriate fallback or explicit handling instead of calling get blindly. A consumed stream cannot be reused.

example.title: Select passing exam scores and add a bonus
example.situation: From 40, 70, and 90, keep scores at least 50, add 5 to each selected score, and collect the result.

steps.title: Choose passing values
steps.text: filter keeps 70 and 90; 40 does not pass the condition.

steps.title: Transform the selected values
steps.text: map produces 75 and 95.

steps.title: Collect a result
steps.text: collect evaluates the pipeline and gathers a list. The original marks remain unchanged.

example.change: Change the passing threshold to 80. Predict both printed lists, then write the same transformation using a loop.

check.question: Does calling marks.stream().filter(...) by itself create a result list?
check.answer: No. filter is lazy and returns a stream. A terminal operation such as collect is needed to process and gather the selected values.

java8-features.remember: Read a pipeline one operation at a time and be able to express the same logic with a loop.
java8-features.mistake: Do not assume parallelStream always makes a program faster or makes shared writes safe.
java8-features.ready: You can explain the input and result of each operation in a small stream pipeline.

final-review.title: Final Practice & Review
final-review.goal: Combine Java fundamentals, test your assumptions, and choose a starting point for DSA.
final-review.idea: A complete small program combines familiar parts. Describe the input, choose a representation, divide the work into methods, trace one example, and check boundary cases before optimizing.
words: Follow statements by hand with small input.
A valid input near a limit, such as an empty list.
A fact your algorithm keeps true as it progresses.
focus: Build and trace a small version
Move into DSA when the core is comfortable

concepts.title: Plan before typing
concepts.text: For a spending report, decide whether you need individual entries, a total, or totals per category. State the input rules and required output. Start with a straightforward solution you can explain.

concepts.title: Build and trace a small version
concepts.text: Write one helper for one job. With amounts 20, 30, and 20, trace the running total as 20, 50, and 70. For a frequency map, track the count for each amount separately.

concepts.title: Test boundaries and explain cost
concepts.text: Try no entries, one entry, repeated amounts, and large totals. Decide whether negative amounts are valid. A single scan uses O(n) time; a map holding k distinct amounts uses O(k) extra space.

concepts.title: Move into DSA when the core is comfortable
concepts.text: Begin with complexity, array scans, basic searching and sorting, then binary search and hashing patterns. Continue into two pointers, sliding windows, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, graphs, and dynamic programming in a deliberate sequence. File and concurrency details can be revisited alongside that path.

example.title: Create a daily spending summary
example.situation: A student spent 20, 30, and 20. Use a helper for the total and a sorted map for how often each amount occurred.

steps.title: Represent the entries
steps.text: An int array keeps the individual payments.

steps.title: Summarize the values
steps.text: The method returns a long total. The map counts repeated amounts.

steps.title: Choose deterministic order
steps.text: TreeMap prints keys in sorted order. Each map update costs O(log k), so this complete example is O(n log k), plus the O(n) total scan.

example.change: Use an empty array. Predict the total and map output, then run it. Next add a fourth payment and recalculate by hand.

check.question: Why does the total method work for an empty array?
check.answer: sum starts at zero, the loop runs zero times, and the method returns zero. It never tries to access amounts[0].

final-review.remember: Be able to read input, trace loops, write methods, manipulate arrays and strings, choose collections, and explain growth before tackling harder DSA.
final-review.mistake: Do not move on only because a sample passed. Check edge cases and explain why the algorithm works.
final-review.ready: You can build and debug a small program from a blank editor and explain its time and space usage.
